questions.question: For $v=(v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n)$, what is meant by the $i$th coordinate of $v$?
options: The number of nonzero entries before $v_i$.
The norm of the vector.
The index $n-i$.
The entry $v_i$.

questions.question: How many coordinates does a vector in $\mathbb R^n$ have?
options: It depends on how the vector is drawn.

questions.question: Why does the order of coordinates matter in $(v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n)$?
options: Only the largest coordinate matters.
Changing the order can give a different vector.
The order matters only for zero vectors.
Coordinates are treated as an unordered set.

questions.question: What information is contained in the coordinate $v_2$ of a vector $v$?
options: The final entry of the vector.
The second entry of the vector.
The dimension of the vector space.
The length of $v$.

questions.question: Why do coordinate equations often appear when studying linear combinations?
options: Two vectors are equal exactly when their corresponding coordinates are equal.
Linear combinations do not have coordinates.
Coordinates can only be used for matrices.
The coefficients must be coordinates of the same vector, for every possible choice of input.

questions.question: For $v=(3,-1,4)$, what is the second coordinate?
Which vector in $\mathbb R^3$ has first coordinate $2$ and third coordinate $-1$?
If $(a,3)=(2,b)$ in $\mathbb R^2$, what are $a$ and $b$?
Which vector has exactly four coordinates?
If two coordinate vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ are equal, what must be true of their entries?
options: Only their sums of coordinates must match.
Every corresponding coordinate must be equal.
They must have all coordinates nonzero.
Only their first coordinates must match.

questions.question: Why is $(1,2)$ not the same coordinate vector as $(2,1)$?
options: The first and second coordinates have been interchanged.
Coordinate order is ignored in $\mathbb R^2$.
They have the same two entries, so they are equal.
Both have norm $\sqrt5$, so they must be equal.

questions.question: What does a coordinate description allow us to do with a vector equation?
options: Avoid checking any entries.
Break it into scalar equations for individual entries.
Replace all vectors by their lengths only.
Turn every equation into a determinant.

questions.question: Let $u=(1,2,3)$ and $v=(4,5,6)$. What is the second coordinate of $2u-v$?
For which value of $a$ does $(a,4,1)$ equal $(2,4,1)$?
options: Any real $a$

questions.question: Can two different coordinate descriptions represent the same vector in a fixed coordinate system?
options: Yes; any permutation of the entries represents the same vector.
Yes; any vector with the same length is the same vector.
No; in a fixed coordinate system the coordinates of a vector are unique.
No, because vectors do not have coordinates.

questions.question: Why is it risky to identify a vector only by the set of numbers appearing among its coordinates?
options: The set contains too much directional information.
The set records all coordinate positions exactly.
Vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ are not ordered tuples.
The set loses order and repeated entries.

questions.question: Solve the coordinate equation $(2a-b,a+b)=(1,5)$. What is $a$?
For $v=(1,-2,0,4)$, which statement about its coordinates is correct?
